title: Your strategy's worst drawdown hasn't happened yet. It's still in the future. How do you plan for a pain you've never seen?
author: Electronic_Tea_2948
selftext:
Something backwards I can't resolve. In almost every field, more data equals more certainty. In algo trading, the more I dig, the less sure I get.  
The problem is that markets barely repeat. You get one real path through history, not thousands of clean experiments. So a strategy might have "20 years of data" but only a handful of genuinely independent market cycles inside it, which is a laughably small sample to bet real money on. And the more I test, the more I realize how thin that evidence actually is.  
So how do you make peace with the fact that we're all making high-conviction decisions on tiny effective sample sizes? Do you just size down to survive being wrong, or is there a way to actually get confident I'm missing?

comments.author: CryptographerNo3692
comments.body: yes....appropriate sizing is not a glorious solution but rule #1, survive to trade tomorrow.  Rule #2, diversify

comments.author: AwesomeThyme777
comments.body:
Agreed. One equity curve is just one shuffle of the deck. Your worst drawdown in the backtest is almost never the worst it can actually get.

What actually helped me: freeze entry, exit, and risk first, then run Monte Carlo on the trade sequence so you see a distribution of drawdowns instead of just one random path the market decided on. If the 5th percentile wrecks you, the strategy isn’t sized yet, no matter how pretty the original chart looks.

Stratos is a good place to start because you can lock the rules, backtest, Monte Carlo the paths, then decide if it deserves size all in the same place. [https://www.stratostrading.ai](https://www.stratostrading.ai/)

comments.author: AdBitter6080
comments.body:
You're describing the fundamental mismatch between backtest sample size and live path-dependence. A 20-year backtest on daily data isn't 5000 independent observations — it's 5-8 market regimes (2008, 2011, 2015, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024...). That's your effective sample size.

The way to make peace with it: size for the worst regime you *didn't* see, not the worst one you did.

Practical framework I use:
1. Segment your backtest by regime (vol, trend, correlation). You'll usually find 2-3 regimes where the strategy was flat or slightly negative.
2. Take the worst regime's max drawdown, multiply by 1.5-2x (unseen regime buffer).
3. Size position so that *that* drawdown = your max tolerable loss (e.g., 5-10% of capital).
4. The rest of the time you're leaving edge on the table — that's the cost of survival.

Alternative: run a stress test with regime-switching Monte Carlo (HMM or k-means on vol/correlation). If 95th percentile drawdown exceeds your limit, reduce size until it doesn't. This is the only way to size confidently on 'tiny effective sample sizes.'

comments.author: Exciting-World5861
comments.body: You have to assume that future data will not be radically different to historical data. And if your strategy holds up in a long period of backtesting, then it will hold up live. That's the leap of faith you have to make, and why backtesting is so fundamental.
